valuation.say: Alright, this is Module 4, Valuation, and we open with how a bond is priced. A bond is worth the present value of the cash it will pay you, every coupon plus par at maturity, discounted at today's market yield for similar bonds. The coupon is fixed at issue, so when market rates move, price is the only thing that can adjust. That's why price and yield always move in opposite directions. Market rate above the coupon, it's a discount bond; below the coupon, a premium. Walk Corinne's bond: fifteen years, a thousand par, four percent coupon paid semiannually, and comparable bonds yield five and a half. Predict first: market above coupon, so expect a discount. On the calculator with two payments per year, N is thirty, I over YR is five point five, payment is twenty, future value a thousand. Solve, and the price is eight hundred forty-eight thirteen. Then yield rankings. Current yield is coupon over price and ignores the trip back to par. For a premium bond, current yield is highest, yield to maturity in the middle, and yield to call lowest, because a call makes you absorb the premium loss sooner. For a discount bond it flips: yield to call highest, current yield lowest. The exam trap: for a bond you already own, price it on its remaining term at today's yield for that term, not the original maturity or original yield. To a client: your coupon never changes, so if new bonds pay more, your bond's price drops until a buyer earns the same as on a new one, and if rates fall, the reverse happens.

Duration. It's the weighted-average time, in years, until you collect a bond's cash flows, measured in present-value dollars. Picture a seesaw holding each discounted cash flow; the balance point is the duration. Because it captures both timing and size, it's also the standard gauge of interest-rate risk, the bond market's cousin of beta. Now the drivers. Higher coupon, lower duration. Higher market yield, lower duration. Longer maturity, higher duration. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, so it's longer than any coupon bond of the same maturity, and a coupon bond's duration is always shorter than its maturity. The Board uses Macaulay duration; the textbook names modified duration but says you won't compute it separately. Walk the cash-flow method: a three-year, six percent annual coupon bond at a seven percent yield. The present values are fifty-six oh seven, fifty-two forty-one, and eight sixty-five twenty-eight, which add up to a price of nine seventy-three seventy-six. Multiply each by its year, sum to two thousand seven fifty-six seventy-one, and divide by the price: two point eight three years, shorter than the three-year maturity, as it must be. Divide by price, not par. For immunization, match duration, not maturity, to the horizon: given a horizon and a list of bonds, pick the duration closest and ignore the maturities. The trap: raising the coupon or the market yield shortens duration; only maturity moves the same direction. And a bond fund never matures, so its duration-driven price swings are real. To a client: your goal is about nine years out, so we'll hold bonds with duration near nine, so price swings and reinvestment roughly offset by the time you need the money.

Now duration in action: estimating how much a price moves. The quick rule of thumb says the percent change in price is about negative duration times the change in yield. The textbook's more precise version divides that rate change by one plus the current yield to maturity. Walk Nadia's bond: price nine eighty, duration six point two, yield five percent, and rates rise seventy-five basis points. Point oh oh seven five divided by one point oh five is about point oh oh seven one four. Times negative six point two, that's about minus four point four three percent. Times nine eighty, a drop of about forty-three forty, so the new price is about nine thirty-six sixty. The rule of thumb alone would say minus four point six five percent. So which one? If the question supplies the current yield and wants an exact estimate, use the one-plus-y version; if it asks approximately with no yield given, use the rule of thumb. For semiannual bonds, halve the yield in the denominator but keep duration and the rate change as they are. The mistakes: plugging in the coupon rate for y, forgetting the divisor, adding when rates rise, and halving the rate change too. The exam trap: the coupon rate is already baked into duration, so it never goes into the price-change formula. To a client: this fund's duration is about thirteen, so a one-point rate rise means roughly a thirteen percent drop, versus two or three percent for the short fund. That extra yield comes with about ten points more downside. Is that a trade you're comfortable with?

Convexity fixes duration's blind spot. Duration draws a straight line through what's really a curved price-yield relationship. For small rate moves, generally under one percent, the line is close enough. For bigger moves the curve matters, and convexity measures the gap between the curve and the line. Positive convexity is typical of straight, noncallable bonds: when rates fall, gains beat the duration estimate, and when rates rise, losses are smaller than it predicts. Heads I win more, tails I lose less. Negative convexity shows up in callable and mortgage-backed bonds, and it flips: gains lag and losses exceed the estimate. Why? Anything the issuer can call or the borrower can prepay caps the upside. Convexity is highest with low coupons, low yields and long maturities, the same pattern as duration. Walk the example: a noncallable bond with duration six, and rates move two and a half points. Duration alone says plus or minus fifteen percent. If rates fall, positive convexity means the actual gain is more than fifteen. If rates rise, the actual loss is less than fifteen. Swap in a callable bond with the same duration and it's the opposite: gain less than fifteen, loss more than fifteen. The exam trap: the Board doesn't expect a convexity calculation, only its direction. Duration understates price increases and overstates price decreases for positively convex bonds. To a client: this callable bond pays a bit more, but if rates fall the issuer can call it, so it won't rise much, and if rates rise it can fall harder. You're being paid extra yield for giving the issuer that option.

Fundamental analysis. The idea is to estimate a security's intrinsic value from economic, industry and company data, then look for a gap versus the market price. The raw materials are the financial statements. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at one point in time. The income statement shows income and expenses over a period. The statement of cash flows ties the income statement to the change between two balance sheets. Book value is assets minus liabilities, and divided by common shares it's book value per share; it's based on historical cost, so it's rarely fair market value. Now the ratio families. Liquidity: the current ratio is current assets over current liabilities, and the quick ratio takes inventory out first. Profitability: net margin, return on assets, return on equity. Leverage: debt-to-equity and debt-to-capital. And times interest earned is EBIT over annual interest. Walk Brightwater: current assets four hundred fifty thousand, including a hundred fifty thousand of inventory, and current liabilities three hundred thousand. Current ratio, one point five. Quick ratio, four fifty minus one fifty over three hundred, one point oh. Book value per share: two point four million of assets minus point nine million of liabilities, over three hundred thousand shares, five dollars. The exam traps: notes payable and accounts payable are liabilities, not assets, and one ratio alone means little, so compare over time and against peers. To a client: before recommending a company, I check whether it can pay its bills, how efficiently it runs, what it earns on its capital and how much debt it carries, and I compare that with its competitors.

Technical analysis. Chartists study only past price and volume to read demand and forecast direction; they care what trades happened, not why. They assume supply and demand alone set prices, prices move in persistent trends, and shifts show up in price action early. A rise on heavy volume is bullish; a drop on heavy volume is bearish. Now the indicators, and many are contrarian, meaning you do the opposite of the crowd. High mutual fund cash, bullish. A high put-call ratio, bullish. Small investors buying odd lots, sell. Over eighty percent of stocks above their two-hundred-day average, bearish; under twenty, bullish. High short interest versus volume, bullish, because shorts have to buy to cover. Walk the example: an advisor's analysis says Stock Q is cheap after a steep fall. The selection stays fundamental, intrinsic value versus price. Execution can use technicals, like waiting for on-balance volume to start rising or buying near support, because enough technicians act on those signals that their buying can move the price. Then the efficient market link: technical analysis doesn't help under any form of the EMH, and fundamental analysis helps only in the weak form. The exam trap: CAPM's required return uses only the market return, the risk-free rate and beta, nothing about the company. Fundamental analysis supplies a realistic growth rate and can show expected return falling short of required return. To a client: I choose investments based on the business and how they fit your overall mix. Charts don't drive the decision, but I may use them to pick a better moment to buy or sell.

Financial leverage and growth. The mechanism: borrowing shrinks the equity base, so the same earnings look bigger per dollar of equity, and ROE and EPS rise. The price is fixed interest, which lowers net income and becomes a burden in a contraction. ROE is net income over equity; ROA is net income over total assets. Walk it: two firms each raise forty million. Firm X is all equity; Firm Y is fifteen million of equity plus twenty-five million of debt. Each earns four million. X's ROE is ten percent; Y's is four over fifteen, about twenty-six point seven. Now sustainable growth: g equals ROE times the retention rate, and retention is one minus the payout ratio. Halcyon Corp has eight hundred million of assets and three hundred million of liabilities, so equity is five hundred million. Net income of sixty million gives an ROE of twelve percent and an ROA of seven and a half. It pays twenty-four million in dividends, so it retains thirty-six of sixty, point six. Growth is twelve percent times point six, seven point two percent. Cut retention to point four and growth falls to four point eight. More payout, slower growth. The tell: with low debt, ROA and ROE sit close together; with heavy debt, ROA is a small fraction of ROE. A dazzling ROE with a modest ROA means the return is borrowed. The exam trap: high retention is right when the company can reinvest at a high ROE. To a client: this company's forty percent return on equity looks great, but most of it comes from borrowing, and in a recession those interest payments don't shrink.

Intrinsic value models. Intrinsic value is the present value of a stock's expected future cash flows, and you pick the model that matches the cash-flow pattern. Value above price means undervalued; below price, overvalued. A fixed dividend with no maturity, like preferred stock, uses the no-growth model: dividend over required return. Mature companies use the constant growth, or Gordon, model: next year's dividend over r minus g, and g must be below r. Growth-phase companies use a multistage model. Now the multistage example, slowly. Wren Corp just paid a dollar forty, grows eight percent for three years, then three percent forever, and the required return is nine percent. The dividends are one fifty-one, one sixty-three, and one seventy-six. Year four is one seventy-six times one point oh three, one eighty-one. The value at the end of year three is one eighty-one over point oh six, thirty dollars seventeen. Then discount it all: year three's cash flow is one seventy-six plus thirty seventeen, and the net present value at nine percent is twenty-seven forty-one. Next, D zero versus D one. Just paid or currently paying is D zero, so grow it first; expected next year is D one, so use it as is. Arbor just paid one eighty, with five percent growth and an eleven percent required return: D one is one eighty-nine, value thirty-one fifty. The trap: preferred feels safe but never matures, so it carries heavy interest-rate risk. To a client: based on the dividends we expect and the return you need, if the stock trades above what it's worth to you, I'd wait or look elsewhere.

Last section: relative valuation. Instead of building a dollar value from the stock's own cash flows, you compare its price with earnings, growth, cash flow or sales, then benchmark against peers, the industry or the market. Lower than peers generally hints at value; higher hints at overpricing. P over E is price over earnings per share, and value can be estimated as EPS times a benchmark P over E. PEG divides P over E by growth, entered as a whole number, and under one is seen as good value. Price to free cash flow is one plus g over r minus g. Walk Larkspur: price sixty-three, EPS four twenty, industry P over E eighteen. Its own P over E is fifteen, below the industry. Four twenty times eighteen is seventy-five sixty, above sixty-three, so it looks undervalued. Then a PEG screen. Alder is twenty-four over twenty, one point two. Birch is fifteen over ten, one point five. Cedar is twelve over fifteen, point eight. Dogwood is ten over five, two. Cedar is the cheapest for its growth, even though Dogwood has the lowest P over E. How to tell intrinsic from relative: if the method needs a peer benchmark to reach a verdict, it's relative. The exam traps: a lower P over E is not automatically a bargain, because a faster grower deserves a higher one, and a strong price to sales can hide losses. To a client: investors pay fifteen times earnings here while similar companies trade at eighteen, so at the industry multiple the shares would be around seventy-five, as long as there's no business reason for the discount.
